questions.stem: The Yellow River takes its name from:
options: the fields of yellow rice that grow along its banks
the gold dust found in the sands of its upper reaches
the fine loess soil it carries, which colours its water
the yellow robes worn by the priests who worshipped the river god
questions.explanation: The river carries huge amounts of yellow loess silt from the plateau of northern China. The silt made fertile farmland but also raised the riverbed, causing devastating floods.

questions.stem: The Yellow River was sometimes called ‘China's Sorrow’ because:
options: it formed a border that no army or trader was able to cross
its floods and changes of course destroyed farms and villages
its water was too salty to be used for growing any crops
it froze solid each winter and cut the north off from the south
questions.explanation: Silt raised the river above the surrounding plain, so when its banks broke it flooded vast areas and sometimes shifted course entirely. Controlling it became a major task for rulers.

questions.stem: In early China, the main crop of the Yellow River valley differed from that of the Yangtze River valley. Which pairing is correct?
options: Rice in the Yellow River valley; millet in the Yangtze valley
Wheat in the Yellow River valley; maize in the Yangtze valley
Barley in the Yellow River valley; potatoes in the Yangtze valley
Millet in the Yellow River valley; rice in the Yangtze valley
questions.explanation: The drier, colder north suited millet, while the warm, wet south suited rice grown in flooded fields. Maize and potatoes came from the Americas thousands of years later.

questions.stem: Historians once believed Chinese civilisation began only in the Yellow River valley. Which evidence has done most to challenge this view?
options: Bronze vessels from Zhou tombs, whose inscriptions describe grants of land
Complex regional cultures, such as Liangzhu and Sanxingdui, found far from the Yellow River
Oracle bones found at Anyang, which record the questions asked by the Shang kings
The Spring and Autumn Annals, which describe the history of the state of Lu in great detail
questions.explanation: Discoveries such as Liangzhu near the Yangtze delta and Sanxingdui in Sichuan show sophisticated regional cultures developing separately, so civilisation grew in several places that interacted. Anyang is itself in the Yellow River region.

questions.stem: The Erlitou culture, centred in modern Henan from about 1900 to 1600 BCE, is significant because:
options: it was the capital from which Qin Shi Huangdi unified China
its people built the first stretches of the Great Wall
it had palaces and early bronze ritual vessels, signs of an early state
its oracle bones contain the oldest Chinese writing that has ever been found
questions.explanation: Erlitou shows large palace foundations, bronze casting and social ranking, all features of an early state. Whether it was the capital of the traditional Xia dynasty is still debated. Oracle bone writing comes from the later Shang.

questions.stem: Some Chinese scholars identify Erlitou with the Xia dynasty, while others are more cautious. Why does this debate remain unresolved?
options: Erlitou was destroyed so completely that no buildings or graves survive
Erlitou lies in southern China, far from where later texts place Xia
Erlitou dates to after the Shang, so it cannot be the earlier Xia
No writing has been found at Erlitou that names the site or its rulers
questions.explanation: The Xia appear only in much later texts, and Erlitou has produced no inscriptions linking it to that name. The site itself is well preserved, lies in the Yellow River region, and is older than the Shang.

questions.stem: The Shang dynasty ruled in northern China from about:
options: 221 to 206 BCE
771 to 476 BCE
questions.explanation: The Shang ruled from about 1600 BCE until their defeat by the Zhou, now commonly dated to 1046 BCE. 221 to 206 BCE is the Qin dynasty.

questions.stem: Shang oracle bones were usually made from:
options: bamboo strips tied together with silk
polished jade discs and bronze plates
clay tablets dried in the summer sun
ox shoulder blades and turtle shells
questions.explanation: Diviners used cattle scapulae and turtle plastrons. Bamboo strips were used for books in later periods, and clay tablets belong to Mesopotamia.

questions.stem: How were Shang oracle bones used?
options: The bones were ground into powder and mixed with wine for the king to drink
A question was put to the ancestors, the bone was heated and the cracks were read
The bones were thrown into a river, and the way they floated showed the gods' answer
Priests carved a prayer on the bone and buried it under a new house or temple
questions.explanation: Diviners prepared hollows in the bone, applied heat until it cracked, and interpreted the cracks as answers from ancestors or spirits. The question and sometimes the result were then inscribed. Ground ‘dragon bones’ were later sold as medicine, which is how they were rediscovered.

questions.stem: Shang oracle bone inscriptions ask questions such as whether the harvest will be good, whether to attack an enemy, and whether a royal birth will go well. This shows that the Shang king:
options: made all his decisions by vote in an assembly of nobles
relied on written law codes rather than on the ancestors
saw himself as a link between the spirit world and the people
had no interest in war, farming or the royal family's future
questions.explanation: The king consulted his ancestors and the high god Di on matters of state, war and family, acting as chief intermediary between the human and spirit worlds. This gave religious authority to his rule.

questions.stem: Oracle bones are the earliest large body of Chinese writing. What is their main limitation as a source for Shang society?
options: They describe only the Zhou dynasty, which ruled after the Shang had fallen
They record the concerns of the king and court, not the lives of ordinary people
They are written in a script that has no link at all to any later Chinese characters
They were all forged in the nineteenth century to sell to European collectors
questions.explanation: The bones come from royal divination, so they show what mattered to the king: war, harvests, sacrifices and the royal family. Peasants appear only as labour or subjects. The script is the ancestor of modern Chinese, and the bones were excavated scientifically at Anyang.

questions.stem: The late Shang capital, where thousands of oracle bones and royal tombs were excavated, was at:
options: Xianyang
Chang'an
Luoyang
Anyang
questions.explanation: Anyang, the site known as Yinxu (‘the ruins of Yin’), in Henan was the last Shang capital. Xianyang was the Qin capital, Chang'an the Western Han capital, and Luoyang the Eastern Zhou capital.

questions.stem: Shang bronze ritual vessels were produced by:
options: carving solid blocks of bronze with sharp stone tools
melting iron and copper together in a blast furnace
casting molten bronze in clay moulds made in several sections
beating thin sheets of bronze into shape over a carved wooden frame
questions.explanation: Shang craftsmen used piece-mould casting: clay moulds in sections fitted around a core, into which bronze was poured. This needed large, organised workshops, showing the power of the state to control resources and labour.

questions.stem: Bronze vessels in Shang China were used mainly for:
options: offering food and wine to ancestors in rituals
cooking the daily meals of farming families
trading with merchants as a form of coinage
carrying water to irrigate the fields of millet
questions.explanation: Bronze was precious and controlled by the elite, who used vessels such as the ding in ancestral rituals and buried them in tombs. Ordinary people cooked with pottery.

questions.stem: The tomb of Fu Hao at Anyang, found intact in 1976, held bronze weapons and hundreds of bronzes, jades and other objects. Oracle bones name her as a consort of King Wu Ding who led armies. What does this evidence suggest?
options: Women in Shang China were never allowed to be buried with any grave goods
Fu Hao ruled the Shang alone after defeating King Wu Ding in battle
Royal tombs at Anyang contained only the bodies of Shang queens
Some elite women in Shang China could hold military and ritual power
questions.explanation: Weapons in her tomb and oracle bone references to her leading campaigns and performing rituals show that at least some royal women held high status and real power. Her rich grave goods disprove the second option.

questions.stem: Which development in military technology appears in China during the late Shang period?
options: The horse-drawn chariot
The iron sword
The repeating crossbow
The gunpowder-fired rocket
questions.explanation: Chariots appear in late Shang burials at Anyang, used by the elite in war and display. Iron weapons and crossbows became widespread much later, in the Warring States period, and gunpowder came over a thousand years later still.

questions.stem: Human remains found in Shang royal tombs at Anyang show that:
options: human sacrifice accompanied the burial of kings and nobles
Shang kings were buried alone with no grave goods at all
Shang people cremated their dead and scattered the ashes
only farmers were buried at the royal cemetery at Anyang
questions.explanation: Royal tombs held sacrificed victims, including attendants and captives, along with bronzes and chariots. This reflects Shang beliefs that the king needed servants and goods in the afterlife.

questions.stem: The Zhou justified their overthrow of the Shang by claiming that:
options: the people of the Shang capital had voted for the Zhou to rule
Heaven had transferred its Mandate from the corrupt Shang to them
the last Shang king had chosen the Zhou ruler as his rightful heir
the Shang had been foreigners who never had any right to rule
questions.explanation: The Mandate of Heaven held that Heaven granted the right to rule to a virtuous ruler and withdrew it from a wicked one. The Zhou portrayed the last Shang king as cruel and decadent, so their conquest was Heaven's will.

questions.stem: The Mandate of Heaven gave a ruler legitimacy, but it also carried a risk for the ruling dynasty. Which statement best explains why?
options: It gave every noble family an equal right to the throne whenever the king died
It forbade the king from leading armies, so he depended entirely on his generals in war
Disasters or rebellion could be taken as signs that Heaven had withdrawn its support
It required the emperor to give up the throne to his eldest brother every ten years
questions.explanation: Because the Mandate depended on virtuous rule, floods, famine or successful revolt could be read as proof that a dynasty had lost it. Later rebels used the same idea to justify overthrowing their rulers.

questions.stem: In the Western Zhou, the king granted land to relatives and allies, who ruled it in return for loyalty and military support. This system is often described as:
options: Confucian, or the examination system
feudal, or the fengjian system
Legalist, or the junxian system
imperial, or the tribute system
questions.explanation: Under fengjian, the Zhou king enfeoffed kinsmen and allies with territories. The junxian system of commanderies and counties ruled by appointed officials was developed in the Warring States and imposed across China by the Qin.

questions.stem: Under the Zhou, the state came to be seen as more than the person of the king. Which development best shows this?
options: The king handed all government to a council of priests who were chosen by lot
The Zhou abolished all titles and offices and governed only through military force
Officials with defined roles ran government, as bronze inscriptions of appointments show
Every decision was made by the king alone after consulting the oracle bones on each issue
questions.explanation: Zhou bronze inscriptions record appointment ceremonies and official duties, showing a structured administration acting on the king's behalf. This marks a shift towards seeing the state as a bureaucratic institution.

questions.stem: In 771 BCE the Western Zhou came to an end when:
options: the capital near modern Xi'an was sacked and the court moved east to Luoyang
the state of Qin conquered all the other states and declared itself an empire
the Shang returned from exile and recaptured their capital at Anyang
a flood of the Yangtze River destroyed the capital and the royal tombs
questions.explanation: Invaders allied with rebellious nobles killed King You and sacked the western capital. The Zhou court re-established itself at Luoyang, beginning the Eastern Zhou, when royal power was far weaker.

questions.stem: The Spring and Autumn Period is named after:
options: the two harvests that farmers gathered every year
a poem written by Confucius about the changing seasons
a chronicle of the state of Lu that covers these years
the two seasons when the Zhou king held court each year
questions.explanation: The Spring and Autumn Annals is a chronicle of the state of Lu, traditionally linked to Confucius as editor. The period takes its name from this text.

questions.stem: During the Spring and Autumn Period, the Zhou kings still held a ritual position but had little real power. Real power lay with:
options: the emperors of the Qin, who ruled from Xianyang
an assembly of farmers elected from every village
the rulers of large states, some recognised as hegemons
the priests who read oracle bones at the royal court
questions.explanation: Strong states such as Qi and Jin dominated, and their rulers were sometimes recognised as hegemons (ba), who led alliances in the king's name. Duke Huan of Qi was the first. The Qin empire came much later.

questions.stem: Which combination best explains the decentralisation of Zhou power during the Spring and Autumn Period?
options: Confucius persuaded the rulers of the states to give their land back to the king
Expansion created large, distant states whose rulers grew stronger than the king
The Zhou kings defeated every rival and ruled all the states directly from Luoyang
The states agreed to abolish their armies and leave defence to the Zhou king
questions.explanation: As Zhou territory expanded, the regional states became powerful in their own right, absorbed weaker neighbours and competed for hegemony. The fengjian bonds weakened over generations. Confucius held no such power over rulers.

questions.stem: The shi were a social group that grew in importance in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. They were:
options: the high priests of the Zhou court who performed sacrifices to Heaven
lower-ranking members of the elite who served as officials, soldiers and advisers
foreign merchants who controlled the trade along the Yellow River and its many canals
slaves captured in war and forced to work on the royal estates and tombs
questions.explanation: The shi were educated men of lower aristocratic rank who served rulers through ability rather than high birth. Confucius was a shi, and many thinkers of the Hundred Schools came from this class.

questions.stem: The Warring States Period began after the large state of Jin was partitioned into three new states. These were:
options: Yan, Lu and Song
Shang, Zhou and Xia
Han, Zhao and Wei
Qin, Chu and Qi
questions.explanation: The great families of Jin divided it into Han, Zhao and Wei. Together with Qin, Chu, Qi and Yan, they made up the seven major warring states.

questions.stem: Which change in warfare marked the Warring States Period?
options: An end to fighting as states settled all their disputes before the Zhou king
Armies made up only of foreign soldiers hired from beyond the northern frontier
Large infantry armies of conscripted peasants armed with crossbows and iron weapons
Small battles fought only between noble charioteers following strict rules of honour
questions.explanation: States mobilised hundreds of thousands of conscripted peasants, using crossbows, iron weapons and, later, cavalry. Chariot warfare by nobles bound by codes of honour was typical of earlier periods.

questions.stem: Shang Yang's reforms in the state of Qin in the fourth century BCE included rewards for military success, harsh punishments, and grouping households to report each other's crimes. Their main effect was to:
options: make Confucian ritual the basis of all law and punishment in Qin
reduce the size of Qin's army so that farmers could return to their fields
weaken the hereditary nobility and tie peasants directly to the state
restore the power of noble families who had ruled Qin under the Zhou
questions.explanation: Ranks were earned through military merit and farming output rather than birth, and mutual responsibility made every household answerable to the state. This created the disciplined, centralised Qin that later conquered its rivals. The reforms were Legalist, not Confucian.

questions.stem: The Dujiangyan irrigation system, built in the state of Qin about 256 BCE under the governor Li Bing, was significant because it:
options: protected the Qin capital from attack by flooding the plain
supplied drinking water to the tomb builders at Xi'an
turned the Sichuan basin into rich farmland that fed Qin's armies
joined the Yellow River and the Yangtze River with a single long canal
questions.explanation: By dividing the Min River rather than damming it, Dujiangyan controlled floods and watered a vast plain, making Sichuan a granary for Qin's wars of unification. It is still in use today.

questions.stem: In which year did the state of Qin complete its conquest of the other states and create the first unified Chinese empire?
options: 260 BCE
206 BCE
771 BCE
221 BCE
questions.explanation: King Zheng of Qin completed the conquest of the last rival state, Qi, in 221 BCE and took the title Qin Shi Huangdi. 260 BCE was the Battle of Changping, a decisive earlier victory over Zhao.

questions.stem: Why was the Qin victory over Zhao at the Battle of Changping in 260 BCE so significant?
options: It destroyed the army of Qin's strongest rival and opened the way to unification
It ended the Zhou dynasty and moved the royal capital from Luoyang to Xianyang
It was the first battle in Chinese history in which horses were used at all
It led Qin to abandon Legalism and adopt Confucianism as its state philosophy
questions.explanation: Zhao was one of Qin's most powerful rivals, and its crushing defeat removed a major obstacle to Qin expansion. Horses and chariots had been used for many centuries, and Qin remained Legalist.

questions.stem: Which thinker taught that society would be harmonious if people practised ritual propriety (li), humaneness (ren) and respect for parents (xiao)?
options: Laozi
Mozi
Han Feizi
Confucius
questions.explanation: Confucius stressed virtue, ritual and proper relationships, especially filial piety, as the basis of good government. Laozi taught following the Dao, Mozi impartial care for all, and Han Feizi strict law.

questions.stem: The Daoist idea of wu wei, found in the Daodejing attributed to Laozi, means:
options: loving all people equally rather than favouring one's family
acting without forcing things, in harmony with the natural way
ruling through strict laws and severe punishments for crimes
performing every ritual exactly as the ancestors had laid down
questions.explanation: Wu wei, often translated ‘non-action’ or ‘effortless action’, means not striving against the Dao. Strict laws describe Legalism, exact ritual Confucianism, and equal love Mohism.

questions.stem: Legalist thinkers such as Han Feizi argued that a state should be governed through:
options: universal love for all people and the rejection of offensive warfare
clear laws, firm rewards and harsh punishments enforced by the ruler
the moral example of a virtuous ruler and the practice of proper rituals
minimal government that leaves people free to follow the natural way
questions.explanation: Legalists believed people act from self-interest, so order comes from strict law, rewards and punishments. Moral example is Confucian, minimal government is Daoist, and universal love is Mohist.

questions.stem: Mencius and Xunzi were both followers of Confucius but disagreed on one central question. What was it?
options: Whether rulers should govern through moral example
Whether human nature is basically good or basically bad
Whether the Zhou king should rule the states directly
Whether rituals should be performed for one's ancestors
questions.explanation: Mencius held that human nature is good and needs nurturing; Xunzi held that it is bad and must be shaped by ritual and education. Both valued ritual and virtuous rule. Xunzi's pupils included the Legalists Han Feizi and Li Si.

questions.stem: Mozi's teachings differed from those of Confucius because Mozi:
options: argued that elaborate funerals and long mourning were the highest duty
urged impartial care for all people rather than graded love starting with family
taught that all people should obey strict laws enforced by severe and certain punishments
taught that rulers should avoid all action and leave people to themselves
questions.explanation: Mozi argued for jian ai, impartial care, and criticised Confucian emphasis on family-centred love and costly rituals such as lavish funerals. He also opposed wars of aggression.

questions.stem: Which statement reflects a key idea in The Art of War, attributed to Sunzi (Sun Tzu)?
options: A ruler should never go to war, because all war offends Heaven
Victory depends mainly on asking the ancestors through oracle bones
All warfare is based on deception, and the best victory avoids battle
Wars are won by the side with the most chariots, whatever the plan
questions.explanation: The Art of War stresses deception, knowing yourself and your enemy, and winning without fighting where possible. It treats war as a matter of strategy, not numbers or divination.

questions.stem: Why did so many schools of philosophy flourish in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods?
options: Buddhist monks arriving from India encouraged debate in the courts of the states
Competing rulers sought advisers with new ideas on how to restore order and win power
The Zhou king ordered every scholar to write a book on how best to govern his many lands
A single empire with peace and wealth gave scholars time to write and to travel
questions.explanation: Political disorder and competition between states created demand for advisers who could offer ways to govern, strengthen the state or end chaos. China was not unified until 221 BCE, and Buddhism arrived centuries later.

questions.stem: By the Warring States Period, Chinese metalworkers were producing cast iron. This development mattered because it:
options: replaced bronze in all ritual vessels used in ancestor worship
was used mainly to make coins for trade with the Roman Empire
allowed builders to make the first steel bridges over rivers
made strong tools and weapons cheaper and more widely available
questions.explanation: Cast-iron ploughshares, hoes and weapons could be produced in large numbers, raising farm output and equipping mass armies. Bronze continued to be used for ritual vessels, and contact with Rome came much later.

questions.stem: Before unification, states such as Qi and Zhao used bronze money cast in the shape of:
options: fish and birds
squares and stars
shells and pearls
spades and knives
questions.explanation: Spade money and knife money, modelled on tools, circulated in different Warring States regions. The Qin later standardised currency with a round coin with a square hole.

questions.stem: The Spring and Autumn Annals record events in very brief entries, such as wars, treaties and eclipses. Which is the best use a historian can make of this source?
options: Studying the emotions and private thoughts of the rulers of each state
Reconstructing the design of Shang tombs excavated at the city of Anyang
Building a chronology of political events among the states of the period
Learning about the daily lives of peasants working in the fields of Lu
questions.explanation: The Annals give a dated record of diplomacy, war and natural events from the viewpoint of the state of Lu, making them valuable for chronology. Their terse entries reveal little about ordinary people or rulers' inner thoughts.
